extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate literature students; readers studying genre and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate the defining features, subtypes, and critical concepts of comedy and tragedy as presented in a literature/lecture overview. Emphasizes Aristotelian and Hegelian criteria and subtype characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: rise in fortune of a sympathetic central character
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedy is a story of the rise in fortune of a sympathetic central character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happy ending is all that's required; comedy depends more on conventions and expectations of plot and character than on necessarily being funny. (Origin note: linked historically to festive rituals.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic hero: minimally sympathetic character
rubrics_metrics.description: The main character in a comedy must display at least the minimal level of personal charm or worth needed to win the audience's basic approval and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not require a spotless hero—likeable rogues or fun-loving scamps (e.g., Falstaff, Huck Finn) are acceptable; the triumph of an utter villain or completely worthless person is not comical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characters: average or ordinary people
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedies traditionally concern the exploits of ordinary people (lower/middle-income figures, students, tradespeople) rather than kings or heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic plots tend to involve everyday problems (romantic troubles, jobs, exams, money, coping with a bad day). The hallmark can be the audience's satisfaction at seeing deserving people succeed rather than overt laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farce: zaniness, slapstick, and improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce is identified by zaniness, slapstick humor, and hilarious improbability; characters are typically fantastic or absurd and plots full of wild coincidences and endless twists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for elaborate comic intrigues with deception, disguise, and mistaken identity (examples: Comedy of Errors, Pink Panther, Marx Brothers, Three Stooges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic comedy: love plot with obstacles and a happy wedding ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic comedy centers on a love plot in which two sympathetic, well-matched lovers are kept apart by complicating circumstances until they are united or reconciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical features: young, likeable lovers, obstacles (class differences, parental interference, prior relationships), and a fairy-tale-style happy ending—wedding-bells are practically mandatory (examples: Much Ado About Nothing, Cinderella, Guys and Dolls, Sleepless in Seattle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical comedy (including black comedy): targeting vice and folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical comedy's subject is human vice and folly; characters include con-artists, tricksters, hypocrites, and their gullible victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These comedies may trace a rising fortune but often feature cynical or morally corrupt figures; extreme forms (black comedy) invite laughter at mortifying or grotesque events (examples: Aristophanes' The Birds, Ben Jonson's Volpone; films like Fargo, Pulp Fiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian tragedy: downfall of a basically good person through fatal error
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy depicts the downfall of a basically good person through some fatal error or misjudgment, producing suffering and insight in the protagonist and arousing pity and fear in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy aims to effect catharsis—purging pity and fear by arousing them and allowing the audience relief or exhilaration afterward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should evoke pity and fear (catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true tragedy should evoke pity and fear on the part of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: pity and fear are natural responses to spectacles of suffering that could happen to any person; tragedy purges these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero must be essentially admirable and good
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero must be essentially admirable and good; the fall of a scoundrel evokes applause rather than pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nobler and more admirable the protagonist, the greater the audience's anxiety or grief at his or her downfall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downfall must result from a personal error or decision (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a true tragedy the hero's demise must come as a result of some personal error or decision; authentic tragedy is not merely blind accident or pure bad luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic hero must bear some responsibility for his or her own doom; hamartia can be a simple miscalculation rather than an overwhelming 'fatal flaw.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (tragic recognition or insight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anagnorisis: a moment of clairvoyant insight or understanding in which the tragic hero suddenly comprehends the web of fate he has entangled himself in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognition is a key structural moment in many Aristotelian tragedies and often accompanies or precedes catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (tragic error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamartia: a fatal error or simple mistake on the part of the protagonist that eventually leads to the final catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia literally refers to 'missing the mark'—it need not be an egregious moral flaw but can be an inescapable slip-up or misjudgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hubris (violent transgression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hubris: the sin par excellence of the tragic or over-aspiring hero; often translated as 'pride' but better understood as insolent daring or haughty overstepping of cultural/ethical boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hubris commonly precipitates nemesis in tragic narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nemesis (retribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nemesis: the inevitable punishment or cosmic payback for acts of hubris.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as the moral or cosmic consequence in tragic plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (plot reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia: a pivotal or crucial action by the protagonist that changes his situation from seemingly secure to vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often marks the turning point leading toward catastrophe in tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hegelian tragedy: conflict between two rights or values
rubrics_metrics.description: Hegelian tragedy is defined as a dynamic contest between two opposing forces—two esteemed values or rights in fatal conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy (for Hegel) is most tragic when 'good is up against good'—when two legitimate claims cannot be reconciled and one must give way (example: Antigone's religious/familial duty vs. civic duty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenge tragedy: dramatization of a wronged hero seeking justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenge tragedy dramatizes the predicament of a wronged hero who, when legal or social justice fails, must decide whether to take justice into his or her own hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical scenarios involve brutal wrongs allowed to go unpunished and the protagonist's choice to pursue private vengeance (examples: Agamemnon, Medea, Hamlet, Titus Andronicus; modern analogues in Death Wish and many thrillers).
